'''Charles Chapman Pugh''' (born June 16, 1940) is an American mathematician who researches dynamical systems.
Pugh received his PhD under [[Philip Hartman]] of [[Johns Hopkins University]] in 1965, with the dissertation ''The Closing Lemma for Dimensions Two and Three''.<ref>{{MathGenealogyProject|id=25180|name=Charles C. Pugh}}</ref> He has since been a professor, now emeritus, at the [[University of California, Berkeley]].

In 1967, he published a ''[[Pugh's closing lemma|closing lemma]]'' named after him in the theory of dynamical systems.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Bonatti|first=Christian|date=2008-06-10|title=Pugh closing lemma|journal=Scholarpedia|language=en|volume=3|issue=6|pages=5072|doi=10.4249/scholarpedia.5072|bibcode=2008SchpJ...3.5072B |issn=1941-6016|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Pugh|first=Charles C.|date=1967|title=An Improved Closing Lemma and a General Density Theorem|journal=American Journal of Mathematics|volume=89|issue=4|pages=1010–1021|doi=10.2307/2373414|issn=0002-9327|jstor=2373414}}</ref> The lemma states: Let ''f'' be a [[diffeomorphism]] of a compact manifold with a [[nonwandering]] point ''x''.<ref>Wandering points were introduced by [[George Birkhoff]] to describe dissipative systems (with chaotic behavior). In the case of a dynamical system given by a map ''f'', a point wanders if it has a neighborhood ''U'' which is disjoint to all of the iterations of the map on it: <math>f^n(U) \cap U = \varnothing.\,</math></ref> Then, there is (in the space of diffeomorphisms, equipped with the <math>C^1</math> topology) in a neighborhood of ''f'' a diffeomorphism ''g'' for which ''x'' is a periodic point. That is, by a small perturbation of the original dynamical system, a system with periodic trajectory can be generated.

In 1970, he was an invited speaker at the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] in Nice, delivering a talk on ''Invariant Manifolds''. 
[[File:Cartwright pugh 1970.jpg|thumb|[[Mary Cartwright]] (left) with Charles Pugh, Nice, 1970]]
